title: What happened to the twelve
hookLine: church traditions send Thomas to India, Andrew to Greece, James to Spain; tradition says many died as martyrs

cards: Near the end of Mark's Gospel, the King James Bible gives the mission of the eleven in one line: "And they went forth, and preached every where." A short sentence for a very long road.

After it, the New Testament mostly follows Peter and Paul, and the rest of the twelve slip out of the story. Andrew, who went and found his brother Simon. Thomas, who wouldn't believe until he saw the wounds.
Bartholomew, Matthew, Thaddaeus, Simon the Canaanite. The Bible doesn't say where they went. But the churches didn't forget, and some still tell which apostle brought them the faith.

teach.b: The word is tradition: something handed on, from one person to the next. Paul uses it plainly: "hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle."
And the stories of the twelve came down mostly by word of mouth.
Tradition says Thomas went east as far as India, and Christians in Kerala, in the south of India, call themselves Saint Thomas Christians and trace their church to him.

Andrew went to Greece, and Greek tradition remembers his death at Patras. Spanish tradition links James, the brother of John, to Santiago de Compostela, where pilgrims still walk the long road to his shrine.
And tradition says many of the twelve died as martyrs. Now the honest part.
These are traditions, not chapters of the Bible. Some are old, some grew later, and historians weigh each one on its own.

Apart from Judas, Acts tells the death of just one of the twelve, short and hard: Herod "killed James the brother of John with the sword." The same James; Spanish tradition holds his body was carried to Spain afterward.
Catholic and Orthodox teaching gives tradition real weight alongside scripture; Protestant churches teach that every tradition is tested by scripture.

teach.h: TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: In Acts, before he is taken up, Jesus says: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth."
The traditions are a map of people taking that seriously, and some places on that map are still places where being a Christian costs something.

how: Churches remember the apostles on their feast days, and churches in India, Greece, Spain and elsewhere keep the traditions of the apostles linked to them. Churches also pray, in their services, for Christians who face persecution.

o: something handed on, by word of mouth or by letter
a rule written down in scripture for all churches

games.q: who went where, says tradition — tap the pairs.
p: the shrine at Santiago de Compostela

s: the Bible tells where each of the twelve went
it goes quiet. the stories of where they went come from church tradition.
Saint Thomas Christians in India trace their church to Thomas
Paul says traditions come only by letter
"whether by word, or our epistle" (2 Thessalonians 2:15): by word of mouth too.

games.q: you're one of the twelve. Jesus has said you'll be witnesses to the uttermost part of the earth. Jerusalem is the city you know. what do you do?
o: stay in Jerusalem, where it's familiar.
wait for someone else to go first.
games.why: "they went forth, and preached every where." tradition follows them to India, Greece and beyond, and says many of them died far from home.

practice: Bring to mind Christians somewhere who gather quietly because gathering openly isn't safe, or whose church has been burned: a few people, a borrowed room, a door shut before the reading starts.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words; if you don't, hold them in your attention, like a friend far away who's having a hard time.

wordCard.voice: Tradition. Something handed on, by letter or by word of mouth. Here, the stories of where the twelve went, kept by the churches that remember them.

orig.note: Greek: tradition, what is handed on; the word behind "traditions" in 2 Thessalonians 2:15.

carryVoice: Your line: they went everywhere. The churches still remember who came to them. On we go.
